prompt.context: Your client is Aero Inca – Latin America's 2nd largest airline. The airline has a hub in Mexico City and flies to North, South, and Central America as well as a handful of European and Asian destinations. Recently, a number of smaller airlines have expanded and are flying to North America directly, taking market share from our client and decreasing revenue and profitability (which is heading towards the red).
prompt.question: Your job is to advise on what Aero Inca needs to do to increase revenue.

clarifying_info.a: Customers come from two areas: (1) frequent fliers who depart from Mexico City, and (2) throughput transfers to smaller cities that go through the Mexico City hub.

exhibits.title: Route Data
exhibits.shows: Route and flight data for the Mango, Brazil route and the New York route, including plane capacity, utilization rates, and ticket prices
exhibits.data: Plane capacity: 200 people; Mango route: 2 daily flights, 60% utilization, $500/ticket; NY route: currently 12 flights, 80% utilization, $500/ticket; proposed: add 3 NY flights (total 15), expected utilization drops to 70% across all NY flights, competitive response drops ticket price to $450

framework: Revenue levers: apply a 2x2 product-market matrix — (1) same product/same customers, (2) same product/new customers (e.g. tourists vs. business travelers), (3) new product/same customers (e.g. new destinations to current fliers), (4) new product/new markets
Cost levers: fixed costs (planes — buy vs. lease, hub location, equipment) and variable costs (fuel hedging, labor — unionized vs. non-unionized)
Route profitability: compare contribution from new route vs. routes that must be cancelled to free up aircraft
Mango route optimization: maximize utilization or reduce to one daily flight if combined load exceeds two-flight 60% scenario

questions.prompt: How would you think about increasing revenue for Aero Inca?
questions.guidance: A strong answer structures the revenue opportunity using a 2x2 product-market matrix covering same/new products vs. same/new customers, giving airline-specific examples for each quadrant. It should also acknowledge price as a lever (increasing price or lowering price to drive volume) — a potential gap in a candidate's answer.

questions.prompt: Aside from the revenue side, what else should you think about?
questions.guidance: Cover the cost structure: fixed costs (planes, hub, equipment) and variable costs (fuel, labor). Mention specific cost control tactics such as buy vs. lease decisions for planes, hub relocation analysis, fuel hedging, and unionized vs. non-unionized labor.

questions.prompt: The VP of network design needs to know by end of week whether to increase flights to New York (already served) by adding 3 flights, which requires cancelling the two daily flights to Mango, Brazil. How would you decide?
questions.guidance: Frame it as a profitability comparison: calculate revenue (and profit, since costs are assumed equal) for the new NY schedule vs. the current Mango route. Ask for plane capacity, utilization rates, and ticket prices for both routes. Then run the math and compare.

math.setup: Compare revenue from Mango route (2 flights cancelled) vs. incremental NY route (3 flights added, but utilization and price change across all 15 NY flights).
steps: Current NY revenue (before change): 200 × 12 flights × 80% utilization × $500/ticket = $960,000
New NY revenue (after adding 3 flights, 70% utilization, $450 ticket due to competitive response): 200 × 15 × 0.70 × $450 = $945,000
Net change from switching: New NY revenue ($945,000) − Old NY revenue ($960,000) − Mango revenue foregone ($120,000) = −$135,000
Conclusion: switching costs $135,000 in revenue; do NOT switch to the expanded NY schedule
math.answer: Adding the NY flights loses $135,000 in revenue compared to keeping the current routes. Do not cancel Mango.

questions.prompt: If we keep the Mango route, what could the client do to maximize profitability on it?
questions.guidance: First focus on increasing utilization (more passengers per flight). If utilization cannot be improved, look at cost reduction (meals, crew count, lease vs. buy, fuel hedging). If costs are also fixed, consider whether flying only one flight per day is more profitable: at 60% utilization on two flights, the combined load on one flight would exceed 60% and every seat above breakeven is pure profit, potentially outweighing the lost revenue from the second flight. Acknowledge customer ill-will risk of reducing frequency.

math.setup: Compare two-flight scenario vs. one-flight scenario assuming stranded passengers from the second flight are lost.
steps: If all 120 passengers fit on one plane (capacity 200), one-flight revenue: 120 × $500 = $60,000 — WORSE if no extra passengers join

However, if utilization on the combined single flight rises (e.g. 100% of the 60% × 2 = 120 pax consolidate + some new demand), the calculus may favor one flight only if fixed costs per flight (aircraft, crew) are significant

Key insight: above the breakeven load factor, additional passengers are pure profit; reducing to one flight saves one flight's fixed costs but loses passengers who cannot travel — net impact depends on cost per flight vs. revenue from the marginal passengers
math.answer: The one-flight option is worth considering only if per-flight fixed costs saved exceed the revenue lost from passengers who cannot be accommodated. Candidate should flag customer satisfaction risk.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the ways Aero Inca could control its cost structure?

categories.name: Fleet / Capital
ideas: Buy vs. lease aircraft depending on utilization outlook
Sell and leaseback aircraft to free capital
Right-size fleet to actual demand — retire older fuel-inefficient planes

categories.name: Hub & Infrastructure
ideas: Evaluate whether Mexico City hub is optimal or if an alternative hub lowers costs
Share ground-handling equipment with other carriers

categories.name: Fuel
ideas: Hedge fuel prices with forward contracts or options to limit exposure
Build a strategic fuel reserve when prices are low
Invest in more fuel-efficient aircraft over time

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Evaluate union vs. non-union labor cost trade-offs
Reduce non-essential cabin crew on short or low-utilization routes
Cross-train staff to reduce total headcount

categories.name: In-flight & Services
ideas: Unbundle meals — make them paid options rather than included
Reduce galley weight (lighter carts, fewer items) to save fuel
Charge for checked baggage on price-sensitive routes

recommendation: Do not cancel the Mango, Brazil flights to add NY capacity — the route switch would reduce total revenue by $135,000 due to lower utilization and competitive price pressure on the NY route
Focus near-term on improving Mango utilization; if that is not possible, evaluate reducing to one daily Mango flight and reinvesting the freed aircraft in higher-margin routes
On the revenue side, pursue the 2x2 product-market opportunities — particularly selling to new customer segments (tourists) and adding new destinations for existing customers
risks: Competitive retaliation on NY route has already been modeled (price drop to $450); further escalation could erode margins further
Reducing Mango frequency risks customer ill-will and could accelerate share loss to competing carriers on that route
Smaller airlines expanding to North America will continue to pressure pricing — a pure revenue-growth strategy may be insufficient without parallel cost reduction
next_steps: Analyze full cost structure per route to validate the 'costs are a wash' assumption
Explore marketing and loyalty programs to boost utilization on Mango and other underperforming routes
Assess whether hub realignment or fleet optimization could structurally improve the cost position
